drug_class: BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor (a type of targeted cancer therapy)
purpose: Bosutinib is used to treat a type of blood cancer called chronic myelogenous leukemia, or CML. It is typically used in adults whose cancer has come back, stopped responding to other treatments, or who cannot tolerate other CML medicines. It helps control the cancer and keep it from getting worse.
how_it_works: Your cancer is driven by an abnormal protein in your blood cells that tells them to grow out of control. Bosutinib works like a key that blocks this faulty protein, essentially turning off the signal that makes the cancer cells multiply. By blocking this signal, the drug helps slow or stop the growth of cancer cells.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, rash, fever, fatigue, and low blood counts (which can make you more prone to infections, bruising, or bleeding). Many of these can be managed, so let your care team know if they bother you.
warnings: Bosutinib can cause serious liver problems — your doctor will check your liver with blood tests regularly. It can also cause fluid build-up in your lungs or body, serious diarrhea leading to dehydration, and dangerously low blood counts. Tell your doctor right away if you have yellowing of the skin or eyes, shortness of breath, chest pain, or signs of infection. Do not take this medicine if you are pregnant, as it can harm an unborn baby.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 400 mg taken by mouth once a day with food. For newly diagnosed CML, the dose may be 400 mg once daily. For CML that has returned or was resistant to prior therapy, 500 mg once daily is typical. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how well you tolerate the medicine and how well it is working.
